title: I believe, we believe (CCC 166–167)
hookLine: faith is personal but never solitary

lines: A SUNDAY MASS: EVERY VOICE AT ONCE.
cards: A Sunday afternoon baptism. The baby is asleep, or furious.

The priest turns to the parents and godparents and asks, one question at a time, whether they believe in God, the Father almighty, and in his Son, and in the Holy Spirit. Each time they answer out loud: I do.
The next Sunday, at an ordinary Mass, the whole church stands and says the Creed together, every voice at once. Same faith. One time it sounds like a single voice; the next, like a crowd.

teach.h: I BELIEVE: EACH ONE, AT BAPTISM.
teach.b: Day one hundred one took the Apostles' Creed line by line; today, just its first words. The Catechism notices the grammar.
I believe is the faith of the Church professed by each believer personally, above all at baptism; that's how the Apostles' Creed speaks.
We believe is the faith confessed by the bishops gathered in council, or by the whole assembly at worship; that's how the creed of the councils speaks. Both are true at once.
Faith, the Catechism says, is a personal act: a person's free response to God who reveals himself. But it's never an isolated act.
No one can believe alone, it says, just as no one can live alone. Nobody gave themselves faith, any more than they gave themselves life. It was received from others, and it's meant to be handed on.
A moment in Mark's Gospel holds both sides. A father brings his son, who is suffering terribly, to Jesus.

teach.h: I DO BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF.
teach.b: Jesus speaks of believing, and the father cries out, in the Douay-Rheims, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." It's as personal as a sentence can be, and he says it in a crowd, on someone else's behalf, for his child.
The Catechism recalls the baptism rite of the Roman Ritual, where the minister asks what is being sought from God's Church, and the answer is one word: faith.
The Church, it says, believes first, and carries each believer. Even a private prayer, in the Catholic picture, is said inside a very large we.

how: At baptism, the parents and godparents of a child, or the adult being baptized, profess the faith by answering the priest's questions; at Sunday Mass the congregation stands and says the Creed together.

games.q: in the Roman Ritual's baptism rite the Catechism recalls, the minister asks what is being sought from God's Church. what's the answer?
games.why: faith. the Catechism uses the question to show that faith is received from the Church before anyone says I believe on their own.

practice: If you can, say the Creed with someone, at Mass, at home, or quietly along with a recording.
If you're on your own, say or think the first two words, I believe, and let faces come to mind: the people whose faith reached you somehow, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger in a pew.
If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, think of who carried what you know, in any part of life.

wordCard.voice: I believe. The first words of the Creed: personal, said by each one, and never said alone. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: I believe. The first word of the Apostles' Creed in Latin.

carryVoice: Your line: no one believes alone. One voice at a baptism, a crowd on Sunday, the same faith. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief.
